Was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy, though the mother missed several prenatal checkups. The patient's older brother underwent surgery for pyloric stenosis as an infant.

speaker: Doctor
text: Bilious vomiting in a newborn is a surgical emergency until proven otherwise, and gastroenteritis is an incorrect and dangerous diagnosis here. I have requested an abdominal X-ray to evaluate for conditions like malrotation with volvulus. Have you observed any distension of the abdomen, or has the infant passed any stool yet?

text: Past medical history: No significant past medical history. Brother had pyloric stenosis. Social history: NA

speaker: Doctor
text: I note the family history, but pyloric stenosis typically causes non-bilious vomiting, so it does not explain this patient's bilious emesis. REQUEST TEST: Upper_GI_Series

speaker: Doctor

speaker: Patient
text: Physical examination shows epicanthus, upward slanting of the eyelids, low-set ears, and a single transverse palmar crease. A grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur heard at the left mid to lower sternal border. The lungs are clear to auscultation.

speaker: Doctor
text: The physical exam findings of epicanthus, upward slanting eyelids, low-set ears, and a single transverse palmar crease are classic stigmata of Down syndrome. Given the bilious vomiting and this specific phenotype, the most likely diagnosis is duodenal atresia, which is strongly associated with trisomy 21. DIAGNOSIS READY: Duodenal atresia
